Memory Management
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Main Functions of the Operating System (review)
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Memory Management

Its goal is to provide safe, isolated, and efficient memory use for every running process.

Typical tasks:
Memory allocation: assigning memory to programs and processes during execution.
Relocation: mapping a program's logical addresses to physical memory addresses.
Protection mechanisms: preventing a process from accessing another process's or the OS's memory.
Memory deallocation: releasing and reusing memory that is no longer needed.
Address translation: converting logical (virtual) addresses to physical addresses using the MMU.
Virtual memory management: extending physical memory with secondary storage so larger programs can run.
Efficiency: optimizing memory utilization (page replacement, caching, reducing fragmentation).
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Memory Management – Historical Overview
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Fixed Addressing (1950s)

Initially, only one program resided in memory

Programs used fixed addresses
Only one program could run at a time
To run another program, the current one had to be written to secondary storage (swapping)

Advantage: simple and suitable for batch systems
Disadvantage: poor memory utilization and no protection

The program could use the entire physical memory
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Relative Addressing – Static Allocation (early 1960s)

Allowed multiple programs to reside in memory if they fit

When loading programs, the OS added a fixed offset to addresses (programs remained tied to a location)
Programs contain relative addresses
The actual address is formed from the relative address plus the offset
Programs that did not fit in memory waited on secondary storage
The OS swapped programs between memory and secondary storage

Advantages: better memory utilization and easier programming
Disadvantages: more complex implementation, handling multi-part programs, lack of protection
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Relative Addressing – Dynamic Allocation (mid-1960s)

Base and limit registers were added to hardware, enabling dynamic address translation.

For each memory access, the physical address is the logical address plus the base register.
The limit register prevented a program from accessing other processes' memory.
Programs could therefore be relocated during execution
Programs received their own address spaces and no longer saw all physical memory
Basic memory protection was achieved
Address translation became hardware-supported (a predecessor of the MMU – Memory Management Unit)
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Partitioned Systems (early/mid-1960s)

Memory was divided into fixed- or variable-size partitions.

Fixed partitions: simpler, but cause internal fragmentation when a program is smaller than its partition
Variable partitions: more flexible, but may cause external fragmentation when gaps remain between partitions
The OS became responsible for tracking and managing free memory areas

Physical address = 
Base address (partition address) + Logical address (offset)

Management techniques: bitmap, linked list
Algorithms: first fit, next fit, best fit, worst fit
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Segmentation (around 1970)

A program's logical units can be organized into separate segments (code, data, stack, etc.).

Each segment has its own base and limit values.
Hardware support (segment-table management; segment registers: CS, DS, SS, ES)
Permissions can be assigned to segments
Segments can be shared
Internal fragmentation is eliminated, but external fragmentation remains
Can be combined with paging (see next slide)

12.7: Segmentation - Engineering LibreTexts

Logical address = (segment identifier, offset)
Physical address = base + offset
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Paging (early 1970s)

Memory and programs are divided into equal-sized pages and frames.

Page sizes were initially 4 KB or 8 KB, later up to 2 MB
Permissions can be assigned to pages
Goal: eliminate external fragmentation and enable more flexible memory management
The program uses a contiguous address space, while pages may be scattered in physical memory
Address translation uses a page table, which can become very large

Logical address = [page identifier | offset]
Physical address = frame address + offset

Operating System - Memory Management
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Page Tables and Their Implementation

Concept
A page table maps virtual addresses to physical addresses.
Each process has its own virtual address space.
Address translation is performed by the MMU (Memory Management Unit), often accelerated by a TLB.
Implementation
Single-level page table (per process)
Multilevel page table (multilevel index)
Hashed page table (lookup using a hash function)
Inverted page table (stores information about physical frames in one shared table)

OS - 2.6 (MV) (6) Multi-Level Page Tables

Hashed Page Tables in 
Operating System 
- GeeksforGeeks
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Virtual Memory (mid-1970s)

The entire program does not need to be in memory – only currently used pages are loaded.
The MMU (Memory Management Unit) performs address translation; the OS manages page replacement
From the 1980s onward, the MMU became integrated into the CPU
If a page is not in memory, a page fault occurs and the OS loads it from disk.
Internal fragmentation may occur
The apparent memory can be much larger than physical memory.

9_05_PageTable.jpg (720×699)

Physical address = (frame address × page size) + offset
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Modern Memory Management 
(from the 1980s)

Combines paging, segmentation, and virtual memory management

Based primarily on paging with fixed-size blocks
Address translation is performed by the MMU and accelerated by the TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)
Memory protection is especially important
Some pages reside in RAM, while others are on secondary storage (virtual memory)
Segmentation has become less important and today mainly appears logically at the programming level
Various optimization techniques appeared:
Prefetching: loading pages in advance
Memory compaction: reducing fragmentation
Modern page-replacement algorithms
Larger pages to improve TLB efficiency
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Windows 11 – Memory Management

Characteristics
Fully paged virtual-memory system
Each process has its own address space.
Page size: 4 KB (normal), 2 MB / 1 GB (large pages).
Paging file (pagefile.sys)
Stores infrequently used pages on secondary storage.
Copy-on-Write support
When a process creates a new instance of itself, the OS does not copy pages immediately; copying occurs only when one instance writes to them.
Memory compression (since Windows 10)
Separation of kernel and user address spaces – protected kernel memory.
Main components
Memory Manager (ntoskrnl.exe)
Page Frame Number (PFN) Database – tracks RAM pages
Working Set Manager – determines which pages remain in RAM
Standby and Free Lists – manage available pages
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Linux – Memory Management

Characteristics
Full virtual memory; each process has its own 64-bit address space.
Demand paging: only pages actually used are loaded.
Page size: 4 KB (x86_64); huge pages: 2 MB, 1 GB.
Swap partition/file
Copy-on-Write
mmap (memory mapping): a system call that maps a file or device into a process's virtual memory
Shared memory: fast data exchange between processes without files
NUMA support: with multiple CPUs, processes are placed on or near the CPU associated with their memory
Transparent Huge Pages (THP): using larger pages when appropriate
Components:
MMU, TLB – hardware address translation
Kernel Memory Manager (mm/)
Page Cache – file cache
OOM Killer – terminates processes when memory is exhausted
:::


---


::: {.notes}
macOS – Memory Management

Characteristics
Mach-based virtual-memory system.
Page size: 4 KB
Compressed Memory – inactive pages are compressed in RAM.
Unified Buffer Cache – shared file and memory cache.
Copy-on-Write support
Dynamic Pager (swapfile)

Components:
MMU, TLB – hardware address translation
Kernel Memory Manager (mm/)
Page Cache – file cache
OOM Killer – terminates processes when memory is exhausted
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Mobile vs. Desktop OS Memory Management
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Page-Replacement Algorithms

If a new page must be loaded and no free frame remains, the OS must select a page to replace.

Steps:
A program accesses a page not in memory (page fault) → page replacement
The OS must load the page from secondary storage.
If there is no free space in RAM, it must choose which existing page to evict.
The new page replaces the selected page.
If the page was modified, it must first be written to disk.
If it was not modified, it can simply be discarded.
Major page-replacement algorithms:
FIFO, Optimal, LRU, LFU, Second Chance, NRU
:::


---


::: {.notes}
FIFO Algorithm

Characteristics:
Simple queue-based implementation.
Advantage: easy to implement, low overhead.
Disadvantage: Belady's anomaly – more memory (frames) does not always reduce page faults.

Example:
3 frames; page-reference string: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3.

Replaces the page that has been in memory the longest.
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Optimal Algorithm

Characteristics:
Cannot be implemented in real time
Can serve as a reference for other algorithms

Example:
3 frames; page-reference string: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3.

Always replaces the page whose next use is farthest in the future (theoretical
 optimum).

Step-by-step operation
:::


---


::: {.notes}
LRU (Least Recently Used) Algorithm

Characteristics:
Assumes that recently used pages are likely to be used again.
Used in modified/approximate forms by Linux and Windows
A good practical approximation of the optimal algorithm.
Disadvantage: more expensive to implement (requires timestamps or a stack).

Replaces the least recently used page.
:::


---


::: {.notes}
LFU (Least Frequently Used) Algorithm

Characteristics:
Assumes that infrequently used pages are unlikely to be needed later.
Disadvantage: aging problem – old pages may remain because of past usage counts.
Less commonly used in general-purpose operating systems.

Example:
3 frames; page-reference string: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3.

Removes the least frequently used page.
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Second Chance (Clock) Algorithm

Characteristics:
If R=1 → reset it and skip the page;
If R=0 → replace the page.
Fast; approximates LRU.
Implementation: circular buffer (clock hand).


Example:
3 frames; page-reference string: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3.

FIFO-based, but each page gets a “second chance” using an R-bit.
:::


---


::: {.notes}
NRU (Not Recently Used) Algorithm

Characteristics:
Classifies pages into four categories:
(1) not referenced, not modified;
(2) not referenced, modified;
(3) referenced, not modified;
(4) referenced, modified.
Always selects a page from the lowest available category.
Simple, fast approximation of LRU.

Example:
3 frames; page-reference string: 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3.

Uses R (referenced) and M (modified) bits.
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Comparison of Page-Replacement Algorithms
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Page Replacement in Windows

LRU approximation using multiple lists and adaptive page-fault monitoring

Basic principle: an LRU variant using several lists:
Active list: recently used pages
Standby list: older pages still in memory
Modified list: modified pages not yet written out
Free/Zeroed list: free or zeroed pages
The page-replacement approach can be viewed as combining Clock-Pro/LRU-like ideas.
The Windows Working Set Manager manages each process's working set:
removes pages from the working set under memory pressure,
can return them if they are needed again.
It also monitors page-fault frequency (PFF).
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Page Replacement in Linux

LRU-based, two-list, adaptive page replacement

Basic principle: two-list LRU-style implementation.
Active list – recently used pages
Inactive list – older pages; replacement candidates are selected here
Both may contain:
anonymous pages (e.g. heap, stack)
page-cache pages (files, mmap, etc.)
During page reclaim, pages are evicted from the Inactive list.
The kernel uses Clock/Enhanced Second Chance-like techniques:
pages have referenced and dirty flags (R/M-like bits),
pages move between active and inactive lists over time.
Additional modern features:
kswapd daemon – monitors memory pressure and reclaims pages in the background,
zswap / zram – compressed-memory techniques used before or instead of disk swap.
NUMA awareness – preference for process-local, CPU-near memory.
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Page Replacement in macOS/iOS

Two-list LRU-style management + memory compression + priority-based memory
 handling.

In the XNU kernel, page-management logic includes BSD-derived concepts:
Inactive queue + Active queue, LRU-style management.
In modern macOS:
Compressed Memory first tries to compress inactive pages before using disk-backed swap.
Memory is managed with process/task priorities in mind (e.g. foreground vs. background work).
iOS uses Jetsam/memorystatus mechanisms to terminate low-priority apps under memory pressure.
:::


---


::: {.notes}
Comparison of Page Replacement in Modern Operating Systems
:::

NUMA awareness – preference for process-local, CPU-near memory.
:::

::: {.notes}
Page Replacement in macOS/iOS

Two-list LRU-style management + memory compression + priority-based memory
 handling.

In the XNU kernel, page-management logic includes BSD-derived concepts:
Inactive queue + Active queue, LRU-style management.
In modern macOS:
Compressed Memory first tries to compress inactive pages before using disk-backed swap.
Memory is managed with process/task priorities in mind (e.g. foreground vs. background work).
iOS uses Jetsam/memorystatus mechanisms to terminate low-priority apps under memory pressure.
